dimension: Background job engine (lib/jobs + pg_cron tick) — performance, throughput and structural waste
verifier_note: Adversarial re-derivation performed 2026-09-05 07:50-08:20 UTC against live prod (qztcgryhoanennsizcll), read-only SQL only. verified.title: `email_retry_failed` aborts the round-robin in 221 of 288 ticks (76.7%) — the only job type in production that ever leaves a dangling `started` log row
verified.evidence: Re-derived independently on live prod at 2026-09-05 07:55 UTC. (1) Per-tick last-log-row query over job_logs+job_queue, 24h window: `email_retry_failed`/`started` is the final row of 221 ticks; next highest is `email_send`/`retried` at 20, then `email_campaign_process`/`completed` at 15. (2) POSITIVE CONTROL — I ran the inverse query rather than trusting the first: `SELECT q.type, count(*) FROM job_logs s JOIN job_queue q ON q.id=s.job_id WHERE s.status='started' AND s.created_at > now()-'24h' AND NOT EXISTS (terminal row for that job_id)` returns EXACTLY ONE ROW: email_retry_failed = 221. Every other job type in production always writes a terminal row. The query was capable of returning other types and did not. (3) Tick-duration split, bucketing every tick in 24h by whether it ends in a dangling email_retry_failed start: poisoned n=221, mean logged span 10.5s; clean n=67, mean span 39.2s, max 46.3s — the clean figure lands exactly on TIME_BUDGET_MS - MIN_JOB_BUDGET_MS = 40s (processor.ts:72/:86/:152), confirming clean ticks exit on budget as designed. (4) job_queue for this type NOW: 4,684 pending all attempts=0; 930 failed all attempts=5, every one last_error='Timed out in processing; reset by stuck-job sweep'; 2 processing; 4,200 completed (all historical — last completed run_at is 2026-08-17, before the email breakage). (5) Loop site re-read: lib/jobs/processor.ts:150 `for (const type of types)` with `await processSingleJob(job, result)` at :162 — the round is abandoned wholesale when the invocation dies. Handler binding re-checked: handlers.ts:29 `case 'email_retry_failed'` → :172-173 `retryFailedEmails()`.
verified.impact: CORRECTED DOWNWARD from the finder's estimate, which was ~2x inflated. Measured completions: clean ticks average 6.40, poisoned ticks 4.13 (poisoned ticks still do useful work because the poison job is usually not first in the rotation). Marginal loss is 2.27 completions per poisoned tick × 221 = ~502 lost job executions/day, against a ceiling of 288 × 6.40 = 1,843/day and an actual 1,342/day — a 27% throughput loss, NOT the finder's 'well under half' / '1,000+ executions/day'. The non-drainage claim IS confirmed: pending rose 4,492 → 4,684 in the ~19h between the two audits (≈245/day growth against 288/day arrival, so only ~43/day retire via the 5-attempt path). CORRECTION RUNNING THE OTHER WAY: the finder understated the Vercel bill. A poisoned tick stops LOGGING at 10.5s but the function keeps running to its 60s maxDuration, so function-seconds are ≈ 221×60 + 67×40 ≈ 15,900 s/day, not the finder's 6,336 s/day.
verified.recommendation: (1) Fix the handler so it cannot overrun (next finding) — that is the actual root cause and it alone resolves this. (2) Purge the 4,684 pending rows after the handler fix lands, or they replay the same failure 4,684 more times. (3) Treat the processor hardening as a genuine but PARTIAL mitigation and do not oversell it: the finder's suggested `Promise.race` against `remainingTickMs()` cannot cancel the in-flight handler — JavaScript promises are not abortable — so the abandoned job keeps burning the invocation and stays stuck in 'processing' until resetStuckJobs reclaims it. It buys the round the ability to keep claiming other types during the dead SMTP wait, which is worth having, but the real fix is bounding the handler. `lib/jobs/deadline.ts` exports the needed primitive and is imported by exactly one service today (verified: lib/services/sms.service.ts:19, used at :1278 and :1371).
verified.note: Central claim reproduced almost exactly (221/288 = 76.7% vs claimed 226/288 = 78.5%; the small delta is a different 24h window). The dangling-start query is a genuine positive control. Only the throughput-loss magnitude needed correction.

verified.title: `retryFailedEmails()` runs up to 50 serial sends with no deadline check, and each send costs a rock-steady 32.2s because the dead SMTP fallback uses nodemailer's default 30s greetingTimeout
verified.evidence: All three source sites re-read and confirmed verbatim. lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:72-104: `LIMIT 50` at :80, then `for (const log of rows) { await sendTemplatedEmail(...) }` at :86-101 — no import of tickBudgetExhausted anywhere in the file, no per-call timeout. lib/email/provider.ts:70-74: on primary failure, `if (primary.name !== 'smtp' && process.env.SMTP_HOST)` → `return new SmtpAdapter().send(payload)`. lib/email/adapters/smtp.ts:6-16: `nodemailer.createTransport({host, port, secure, auth})` with NO connectionTimeout / greetingTimeout / socketTimeout and no pooling. SMTP_HOST is provably set in prod (554 smtp-provider rows in email_logs in 48h). MY EVIDENCE IS STRONGER THAN THE FINDER'S, which rested on a single trace: I aggregated every email_send execution in 24h from job_logs.duration_ms — email_send/retried n=92 mean 32,254ms (min 32,127, p50 32,228, max 32,680); email_send/failed n=22 mean 32,259ms (min 32,157, max 32,864); email_send/completed n=2 mean 1,122ms. So 114 of 116 executions cost 32.2s with under 1% spread — the signature of a fixed 30s greeting timeout plus ~2s of Resend API round trip, not variance. For contrast, every non-email handler in the same window completes in 387-1,006ms (outbox_dispatch 387, email_campaign_drain 413, sms_retry_failed 414, mpesa_reconcile 1,006). 50 × 32.2s = 1,610s inside a function whose maxDuration is 60 (app/api/cron/route.ts:38, re-read).
verified.impact: Fully explains the tick kill above: the handler cannot complete even TWO sends inside the 60s ceiling, so it can never write a terminal row. Independently, any tick that claims a plain `email_send` loses 32.2s of its 40s working budget (80%) and fails anyway. 452 orphaned smtp/'queued' rows in 48h (rows inserted by SmtpAdapter at smtp.ts:30-33 and never updated) are a separate count of invocations killed mid-greeting-timeout.
verified.recommendation: Three independent breaks, all cheap; do all three. (a) Pass `connectionTimeout: 5000, greetingTimeout: 5000, socketTimeout: 10000` to nodemailer.createTransport in smtp.ts:7 — or simply unset SMTP_HOST so provider.ts:71 stops selecting a fallback with a 0% success rate (554 failures, 0 successes in 48h). (b) Add `if (tickBudgetExhausted(35_000)) break;` inside the retryFailedEmails loop, mirroring lib/services/sms.service.ts:1278. (c) Drop LIMIT 50 to 5. Note (a) is the one that actually matters — with a 5s greeting timeout the same batch costs ~7s/send instead of 32s.
verified.note: Confirmed on better evidence than supplied. The finder's per-send figure (32.7s from one trace) is accurate; the true population mean is 32.25s across 114 samples.

verified.title: The email retry loop is self-amplifying: it re-sent one member's verification email 721 times in 24h, delivering 163 of them, and it is what exhausts the Resend daily quota that then fails every other email
verified.evidence: Live prod re-query, email_logs last 24h grouped by (to, template_key), returns EXACTLY SIX rows in the whole window — confirming the finder's 'only 6 distinct pairs' claim: ezrawafula98@gmail.com/group_verification_link 721 attempts (163 sent, 401 failed, 157 still queued); support@kitabuyetu.co.ke/staff_operational_alert 370 (18 sent); wanyonyipolycarp@gmail.com/weekly_summary 70; Midevabritney@gmail.com/account_statement 12; +2 more with ≤6. Provider/status split over 48h: resend/failed 1,006 all 'You have reached your daily email sending quota.'; smtp/failed 554 all 'Greeting never received'; smtp/queued 452 orphaned; resend/sent 377. THE MISSING GUARD IS REAL AND I READ BOTH HALVES: scheduler.service.ts:71 documents the function as 'status=failed, older than 5 min, fewer than 3 retries', but the SQL at :75-82 filters ONLY on `status='failed'`, `created_at >= NOW()-'24 hours'` and `created_at <= NOW()-'5 minutes'` — there is no retry-count predicate, no per-recipient cap, and no column that could support one. Amplification mechanism verified structurally: SmtpAdapter INSERTs a fresh 'queued' row per attempt (smtp.ts:30-33) and UPDATEs it to 'failed' (:87), so each failed retry mints a NEW failed row that becomes retry-eligible 5 minutes later. pg_stat_user_tables email_logs: n_tup_ins 48,264, n_tup_upd 45,567, n_tup_del 1. Standing backlog: 43,512 'failed' rows against 705 'sent' EVER; 780 rows are retry-eligible at this instant.
verified.impact: Confirmed on all three axes. (1) Quota destruction: the duplicates consume the Resend daily allowance, which is why 1,006 unrelated emails failed with a quota error in 48h. (2) Real user-facing harm — this is the part that most deserves attention: 163 of the 721 attempts to ezrawafula98@gmail.com actually DELIVERED, so one member received 163 duplicate verification emails in a single day. (3) It is the fuel for the two findings above: without quota exhaustion the primary send would succeed in ~1.1s (measured: the 2 successful email_send jobs averaged 1,122ms) and no SMTP fallback would ever be reached. Table growth: 22MB / 48,225 rows on a database whose real business dataset is 9 groups and 37 members.
verified.recommendation: Implement the guard the comment already promises. Without a schema change: in retryFailedEmails, aggregate by ("to", template_key, COALESCE(reference_id,'')) and skip any key already holding >= 3 rows in the window. Better: add retry_count (or original_log_id) to email_logs and UPDATE the original row rather than inserting a new one — that fixes the amplification and the table growth in one move. Independently, treat a quota/429 rejection as a circuit breaker that aborts the remaining batch instead of triggering 49 more attempts. Do this BEFORE purging the job backlog, or the purge just delays the next round.
verified.note: Every element reproduced. Attempt counts differ from the finder's only because the 24h window moved (880 → 721 for the top recipient); the 163 actually-delivered duplicates are a number the finder did not break out and which strengthens the finding.

verified.title: H2 (constant dedup_key) was applied to 4 SMS sweep types and left unapplied to 6 others — those 6 hold 19,729 of the 19,733 pending rows, every one a byte-identical empty payload
verified.evidence: Source re-read line by line. lib/jobs/index.ts:111-131 gives sms_retry_failed (:113), sms_process_schedules (:118), sms_poll_dlr (:123) and sms_release_stale_reservations (:130) bare constant dedup keys. The file's own comment at :107-110 states the mpesa_*/outbox_* sweeps were 'Deliberately NOT applied … not changed blind'; the three email sweeps at :62-79 are not mentioned at all and still carry time-bucketed keys — email_campaign_process (:64), email_retry_failed (:69), email_campaign_drain (:78), plus mpesa_reconcile (:135), mpesa_replay_callbacks (:141), outbox_dispatch (:147), all of the form `type:${dateStr}T${hour}:${fiveMinBucket}`, which mints a new row every 5 minutes regardless of whether the previous one ever ran. LIVE SPLIT, 2026-09-05 07:53 UTC, one query with the payload test built in: the six unconverted types hold email_retry_failed 4,683 / email_campaign_drain 3,731 / email_campaign_process 3,692 / mpesa_reconcile 2,897 / mpesa_replay_callbacks 2,528 / outbox_dispatch 2,198 = 19,729 pending. For every one of the six, `count(*) FILTER (WHERE payload::text IN ('{}','null'))` EQUALS the pending count and `count(DISTINCT payload::text)` = 1 — they are byte-identical duplicates carrying no payload. The four converted types hold 1 row each or zero (sms_poll_dlr 1, sms_process_schedules 1, sms_release_stale_reservations 1, sms_retry_failed 0), exactly the invariant a constant key enforces. The correlation is one-to-one with no exceptions.
verified.impact: 1,728 junk rows/day. Confirmed as the sole driver of job_queue's size — 85,929 rows / 36 MB / 13.9% dead tuples for a system with 9 groups and 49 lifetime payments — and the direct cause of the scan costs in the two findings below. Backlog grew 19,007 → 19,733 in the ~19h between the finder's snapshot and mine, so it is actively compounding, not static.
verified.recommendation: Change the six dedup_key values in lib/jobs/index.ts to the bare type name exactly as :113/:118/:123/:130 already do. All six handlers are payload-free self-idempotent sweeps — I verified this from the data rather than the code comment (distinct_payloads = 1 and empty_payload = pending for all six), which is the property that justified the constant key for the SMS four. Then a one-off `DELETE FROM job_queue WHERE status='pending' AND type IN (...)` keeping one survivor per type. Sequence this AFTER the email handler fix, otherwise email_retry_failed immediately re-enters the same kill loop with a fresh row every 5 minutes.
verified.note: Reproduced exactly, including the payload-identity test. Counts are ~4% higher than the finder's because the backlog grew overnight.

verified.title: The round-robin claim predicate `($2::text IS NULL OR type = $2)` is not sargable — a low-priority single-row claim scans 19,731 pending rows and touches 10,815 buffers
verified.evidence: lib/jobs/db.ts:30-49 re-read: the disjunction is at :40 and the ordering `priority DESC, run_at ASC` at :41. I ran EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE) on the claim's INNER SELECT only — never the UPDATE, since this is production — for sms_release_stale_reservations: `Limit -> Index Scan using idx_job_queue_pick, Index Cond: (run_at <= now()), Filter: (type = 'sms_release_stale_reservations'), Rows Removed by Filter: 19731, Buffers: shared hit=10815`, Execution Time 16.884 ms. The only pending-row index is idx_job_queue_pick (priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status='pending' — it does not contain `type`, so the type test is a post-index filter and the leading priority column forces a scan from the front. pg_stat_statements for the typed claim variant: 22,574 calls, 91,754,087 shared blocks, 4,065 blocks/call lifetime average, max_exec_time 1,963.70 ms — matching the finder's cited figures.
verified.impact: CONFIRMED but with an important nuance the finder missed: 10,815 buffers is the WORST case, not the typical one. Cost depends on the type's priority, because the scan walks `priority DESC` from the front — mpesa_reconcile at priority 10 finds its row almost immediately, while sms_release_stale_reservations at priority 3 must skip all 19,731 higher-priority rows first. The honest production average is the pg_stat_statements figure of 4,065 blocks/call, not 10,815. At roughly 15 claim queries per tick × 288 ticks that is ~17.6M block touches/day ≈ 140 GB of shared-buffer traffic — which happens to land close to the finder's 130 GB/day estimate, so the headline number survives even though the per-call figure behind it was the worst case. The latent-cliff argument is sound: cost scales linearly with backlog depth.
verified.recommendation: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_job_queue_claim ON job_queue (type, priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status = 'pending';` and split the claim into two statements (typed / untyped) instead of the `$2 IS NULL OR` disjunction, so the planner can seek on type. Keep the index after the dedup-key fix — it is what makes the claim path backlog-proof, and it costs almost nothing on a table that should hold ~11 pending rows.
verified.note: Plan shape and buffer count reproduced (10,815 vs the finder's 10,440 — higher because the backlog grew). Per-claim cost re-characterised as priority-dependent; the daily aggregate stands.

verified.title: getDistinctPendingTypes scans all 19,732 pending rows to return 9 strings — but its claimed 902ms/1,594ms cost and 246,528 ms/day are NOT reproducible
verified.evidence: The SHAPE claim is real and I confirm it: lib/jobs/db.ts:57-66, called once per tick at processor.ts:144. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE) on live prod gives `Sort -> HashAggregate -> Index Scan using idx_job_queue_pick, Index Cond: (run_at <= now()), rows=19732, Buffers: shared hit=10809` — 19,732 rows scanned and heap-fetched to produce 9 output rows. THE TIMING CLAIM COLLAPSES UNDER RE-MEASUREMENT. The finder reported Execution Time 1,593.710 ms. I ran the identical statement and got 21.368 ms — a 75x difference with the SAME buffer count and MORE rows. I then re-measured four times back-to-back inside one statement using clock_timestamp(): 0ms, 14ms, 14ms, 17ms. Decisive check on the per-day figure: pg_stat_statements is cumulative, so I differenced it against the finder's own snapshot. getDistinctPendingTypes went 4,353 calls / 3,727,902 ms (finder) → 4,582 calls / 3,731,364 ms (me): +229 calls for +3,462 ms = 15.1 ms per call over the intervening window. The 814ms lifetime mean the finder quoted is a 121-day historical average (pg_stat_statements_info: stats_reset 2026-05-07, window 121 days) and does not describe current behaviour. shared_blks_read = 0 and shared_blk_read_time = 0, so none of this is disk I/O — the historical slowness was CPU contention on the instance, not query shape.
verified.impact: CORRECTED: ~15 ms/call × 288 ticks = about 4.3 SECONDS per day, not the claimed 246,528 ms/day — an overstatement of roughly four orders of magnitude. It is not ~0.9s of every tick's startup either. The index-shape criticism remains valid as a latent issue (a 10,809-buffer scan for 9 output rows is genuinely wrong-shaped and will bite again if the backlog returns), but there is no material DB-time saving to bank here today.
verified.recommendation: Do not justify work with this finding's numbers. The `idx_job_queue_claim (type, priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status='pending'` index from the previous finding makes this an index-only scan for free, and merging this query with getQueueDepth (next finding) is worth doing on its own merits. Both fall out of fixes already justified elsewhere; neither needs this finding to carry them.
verified.note: OVERSTATED, not refuted: the plan shape, buffer count and row count all reproduce exactly. Only the timing and the derived per-day cost fail. The finder read a single EXPLAIN taken during a contention spike as steady state, then multiplied a 121-day-stale lifetime mean by 288. Both pg_stat_statements entries for this query text (mine at 21ms and the finder's at ~1,594ms) are visible in the same row, averaging 814.6ms across 2 calls — which is how a spike this large hides inside a lifetime mean.

verified.title: `getQueueDepth` really does cost ~931ms per tick before any work is claimed, purely to emit one log line — but the figure is ~268,000 ms/day, not 363,000
verified.evidence: lib/jobs/db.ts:89-111, called unconditionally at processor.ts:142 via `await emitQueueDepth()`, BEFORE getDistinctPendingTypes at :144 and before any claim. Same differencing method as above, and this time the cost survives it: getQueueDepth went 601 calls / 757,812 ms (finder) → 830 calls / 970,911 ms (me), i.e. +229 calls for +213,099 ms = 930.6 ms per call in the intervening window. Both queries ran exactly 229 times (once per tick each), so this is a like-for-like comparison against the 15.1 ms/call I measured for its sibling. shared_blks_read = 0 — no disk I/O; the time is CPU. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the live statement: `Sort -> HashAggregate -> Index Scan using idx_job_queue_pick, rows=19732, Buffers: shared hit=10809`, Execution Time 2,106 ms on that run, though a warm back-to-back re-run of the same aggregation completed in 14-17 ms.
verified.impact: CORRECTED to ~931 ms × 288 = ~268,000 ms/day (4.5 min/day) of DB CPU, down from the claimed 363,168 ms/day. MORE IMPORTANT — a structural correction the finder got wrong: the finder billed getQueueDepth at 1,261ms AND getDistinctPendingTypes at 856ms and summed them to '2.1s of introspection per tick'. That double-counts. The two run back-to-back over the same rows, and only the FIRST pays: 931ms for getQueueDepth at processor.ts:142, then 15ms for getDistinctPendingTypes at :144. Real introspection cost is ~0.95s per tick, not 2.1s. The qualitative point stands and is the reason to act: roughly a second of every tick is spent before a single job is claimed, and the starvation detector consumes budget the starving types need.
verified.recommendation: Collapse both into one query — `SELECT type, MAX(priority) AS priority, COUNT(*) AS pending, MIN(run_at) AS oldest FROM job_queue WHERE status='pending' AND run_at<=NOW() GROUP BY type` — and derive both the round-robin order and the depth metric from that single result. Because only the first scan is expensive, merging removes essentially the whole ~931ms rather than half of it. Combined with the dedup-key fix (which takes the scan from 19,732 rows to ~11) this goes to sub-millisecond.
verified.note: CONFIRMED with the magnitude corrected down 26% and the two-query attribution corrected. Note the honest residual puzzle: the identical scan costs 931ms in production ticks and 15ms interactively, with zero disk reads either way. I could not fully explain the gap; what is certain is that the production cost is real, measured over 229 consecutive ticks, and that merging the queries eliminates it regardless of cause.

verified.title: The overwhelming majority of jobs the engine completes do nothing — 957 of 1,342 completions in 24h are provably no-ops, and ~1,251 (93%) almost certainly are
verified.evidence: I did not accept the finder's message list at face value, because half of those messages do not actually state a count. Splitting the 1,342 completions in the last 24h by strength of evidence: (A) MESSAGE LITERALLY REPORTS ZERO — email_campaign_drain 'Email campaign drain (0 sent, 0 failed of 0)' ×188; sms_retry_failed '(0 resolved, 0 still failing)' ×164; sms_release_stale_reservations '(0 consumed, 0 released)' ×103; sms_poll_dlr '(0 delivered, 0 failed, 0 pending of 0)' ×73; sms_process_schedules '(0 schedules, 0 campaigns)' ×60; sms_provider_health 'only 0 message(s) in the window' ×24; disbursement_orphan_monitor 'no stuck payouts' ×24; notify_loan_due_alerts 'no candidates' ×8 = 644, total handler time 364,859 ms. (B) MESSAGE IS SILENT BUT THE SOURCE TABLE IS EMPTY — I checked the tables rather than assuming: email_campaigns has 0 rows, email_campaign_recipients has 0 rows, event_outbox has 0 unprocessed rows. So email_campaign_process ×160 ('Email campaigns processed') and outbox_dispatch ×153 ('Outbox dispatched') are also no-ops, +313 jobs / 121,899 ms. Provable total 957/1,342 = 71.3%, 486,758 ms. (C) SILENT AND UNVERIFIED but near-certain on a system with 49 lifetime payments — mpesa_replay_callbacks ×148, mpesa_reconcile ×122, payment_requests_expire ×24 = 294 jobs / 275,760 ms, bringing the total to 1,251/1,342 = 93%. (D) GENUINE WORK — payment_orphan_monitor ×24, 'Payment spine: 2 ORPHANED payment(s) — staff emailed'. Full aggregate handler time across A+B+C: 762,518 ms/day.
verified.impact: 12.7 minutes/day of handler execution and ~2,500 job_logs inserts to accomplish nothing, plus the claim query behind each one. The finder's 87% headline sits between my provable 71% and probable 93%, and its 682,610 ms/day estimate is if anything slightly conservative against my 762,518 ms. The crowding-out argument is real: these no-ops occupy round-robin slots in ticks that die before reaching the rest.
verified.recommendation: Primarily a cadence problem. Once dedup keys are constant the volume is bounded at one row per type per tick, but 5-minute cadence is still wrong for this system: move email_campaign_drain / email_campaign_process to event-triggered enqueue (both operate on tables that are currently empty), and drop mpesa_reconcile / mpesa_replay_callbacks / outbox_dispatch to 15- or 30-minute cadence. Cheapest complementary change: have each handler return before writing its job_logs rows when its claim query finds nothing.
verified.note: CONFIRMED, with the word 'provably' narrowed. The finder called all 1,088 'provable' on the strength of a '0 sent, 0 failed of 0' message that 607 of them do not carry; I verified those separately against empty source tables and they hold up, so the conclusion survives even though the stated proof did not.

verified.title: job_logs is write-only: 451,892 inserts, 0 updates, 58MB, exactly one application code site (the INSERT), and 52% of rows are content-free 'Starting …' lines
verified.evidence: Full-repo grep for `job_logs` (node_modules excluded) returns exactly one application site: the INSERT at lib/jobs/db.ts:211. Everything else is the creating migration (supabase/migrations/20260526120000_041_job_queue.sql:45,63,92), an RLS deny-all policy (migration 130), DEPLOY.md ops snippets, and other audit documents. There is no SELECT in app/, lib/ or components/. POSITIVE CONTROL: the same grep run for `FROM email_logs` DID find a reader at app/api/v1/email/logs/route.ts, so the pattern is capable of finding a reader and found none for job_logs. Live prod pg_stat_user_indexes: job_logs_pkey idx_scan = 5 against an 11 MB index — nothing reads a log by id; idx_job_logs_job_id idx_scan = 213,828 / 15 MB, which tracks the 317,090 rows deleted via `job_logs_job_id_fkey … ON DELETE CASCADE` rather than any application read. pg_stat_user_tables: n_tup_ins 451,892, n_tup_upd 0, n_tup_del 317,090, 134,803 live rows, 58 MB. Row composition re-counted: started 69,516 (51.6%), completed 65,089 (48.3%), retried 161 (0.1%), failed 36 (0.03%) — only 197 rows (0.15%) carry any diagnostic content. pg_stat_statements for the insert: 451,885 calls, 933,970 ms, 6,032,387 blocks.
verified.impact: ~15.6 minutes of cumulative DB write time and 6M block touches for data no application code has ever read. The 'started' row alone is 69,516 pointless writes. Two INSERTs sit on the critical path of every job (processor.ts:238 and :245), inside the same time budget the starving types are competing for.
verified.recommendation: Stop writing the 'started' row unconditionally — write it only when `job.attempts > 0`, since the attempt counter is its only real content. Then add a retention sweep (`DELETE FROM job_logs WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days' AND status IN ('started','completed')`) or reduce the table to failures only. Keep SOME of the started/completed gap deliberately: it is currently the only record that a job started and never terminated, which is the entire basis of the first finding in this report and the only reason the poison was detectable at all.
verified.note: Every number reproduced within rounding of the finder's (which were ~19h older). The zero-readers claim was checked with a positive control rather than asserted from a negative grep.

verified.title: pruneOldJobs' cleanup DELETE is a full sequential scan and runs 12 times a month instead of once — but it cannot stall the claim path and does not run 'every tick'
verified.evidence: The factual core reproduces exactly. lib/jobs/db.ts:259-267. I ran EXPLAIN WITHOUT ANALYZE (this is a production DELETE — I would not execute it even with a no-match cutoff, which is what the finder did): `Delete on job_queue -> Seq Scan on job_queue (cost=0.00..5275.23 rows=8690) Filter: ((status = ANY ('{completed,failed}')) AND (updated_at < (now() - '30 days'::interval)))` — a full sequential scan, confirming no usable index. idx_job_queue_pick is partial on status='pending' and idx_job_queue_processing on status='processing', so neither serves it. pg_stat_statements matches the finder's figures exactly: 48 calls, 56,213 ms total, mean 1,171.11 ms, max 7,850.63 ms, 35,253 blocks/call. The 12x-per-month claim is confirmed arithmetically as well as by code: lib/jobs/index.ts:340-342 calls `await pruneOldJobs(30)` directly inside `if (date === 1 && hour === 8)`, bypassing the safe()/dedup_key mechanism every other entry in the file uses, so it fires on all 12 five-minute ticks of that hour — and 48 recorded calls over a 121-day stats window is 4 months × 12, an exact match.
verified.impact: CORRECTED — the finder's impact paragraph is wrong in two ways that change the severity. (1) 'A 7.9-second table-wide DELETE holding row locks on the same table every tick' — it does not run every tick. It runs 12 times per MONTH, in a single hour, on the 1st. Between those hours it never executes at all. (2) 'is competing with, and can stall, the claim path' — it cannot. The DELETE takes row locks only on rows with status IN ('completed','failed'), while the claim path selects `status='pending'` under FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (db.ts:38,43). The row sets are disjoint, and SKIP LOCKED means even an overlap would be skipped rather than blocked. The real cost is 11 redundant full-table scans per month that delete nothing, plus one that does — a genuine but minor waste, not a correctness or latency hazard. Downgraded medium → low.
verified.recommendation: Still worth fixing, cheaply: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_job_queue_prune ON job_queue (updated_at) WHERE status IN ('completed','failed');`, and give it a real job type with a `cleanup_old_jobs:${monthStr}` dedup key like every other entry in index.ts instead of the bare direct call, which removes the 11 redundant runs. Batching the DELETE is optional and only matters if the table stays large — after the dedup-key fix it will not.
verified.note: OVERSTATED: plan shape, timings, call count and invocation site all reproduce exactly, but the stated impact ('every tick', 'can stall the claim path') is not true of the code as written, and the finder's own 'plausible cause of a mid-write kill' speculation is inconsistent with its own finding 1, which identifies the actual cause as email_retry_failed on ticks that have nothing to do with the 1st of the month at 08:00.

verified.title: The 'oldest pending job never gets served' premise is wrong — claiming is strict FIFO, the head IS served every tick, and head age equals backlog ÷ arrival rate to two decimal places
verified.evidence: This reproduced more cleanly than any other finding in the set. One query over all six backlogged types comparing MAX(run_at) among completed against MIN(run_at) among pending: the two are ADJACENT 5-minute buckets with no overlap in every case — email_campaign_drain completed through 08-23 08:55 / pending from 08-23 09:00; email_campaign_process 08-23 12:10 / 12:15; mpesa_reconcile 08-26 06:20 / 06:25; mpesa_replay_callbacks 08-27 13:05 / 13:10; outbox_dispatch 08-28 16:35 / 16:40. A clean frontier advancing in run_at order is exactly what strict FIFO produces and is incompatible with the head being skipped. Second proof, computed in the same query: head_age_days versus predicted (pending ÷ 288 arrivals/day) — email_retry_failed 16.27 vs 16.26; drain 12.96 vs 12.95; process 12.82 vs 12.82; mpesa_reconcile 10.07 vs 10.06; replay 8.78 vs 8.78; outbox 7.64 vs 7.64. Six for six to two decimals. The ordering that produces this is `ORDER BY priority DESC, run_at ASC` at db.ts:41 — priority is constant within a type, so it degenerates to pure FIFO.
verified.impact: Correctly redirects the fix, and this is the most valuable finding in the set for that reason. Fairness is already working; a fifth round of scheduler-fairness work (after the four rounds the August incident consumed) would produce nothing. Head age is a pure function of backlog depth and arrival rate, so the only two levers are stopping the tick from dying and stopping the duplicate enqueues — both small, both elsewhere in this list.
verified.recommendation: Do not add another priority or fairness mechanism to the processor. Treat oldest-pending-age as backlog ÷ arrival rate and drive it down by cutting the backlog. Make the starvation detector distinguish the two cases it currently conflates: report `oldest_mins` alongside `completions_in_window` per type, since a type completing >0 with a large oldest_mins is a throughput deficit while a type completing 0 is a genuine stall. As written, emitQueueDepth (processor.ts:194-218) fires logger.error 'queue STARVATION' on any type past STARVATION_MINS = 60 regardless of whether it is draining, which is why the alerts have been misleading.
verified.note: CONFIRMED with the strongest evidence in the report. The six-for-six agreement between observed head age and backlog÷arrival-rate is not something that could occur if claims were being skipped.

verified.title: 100% of pg_cron → /api/cron HTTP calls fail at the pg_net layer while cron.job_run_details reports 288/288 'succeeded'
verified.evidence: Re-run on live prod and reproduced exactly. `SELECT status_code, error_msg IS NOT NULL, count(*) FROM net._http_response GROUP BY 1,2` returns a SINGLE row: status_code NULL, had_error true, n = 72, spanning 02:00:00 to 07:55:00 today — the table's full retention window, and a 100% failure rate with no successful row of any kind. Every error_msg reads 'Timeout of 20000 ms reached. Total time: 20000.126000 ms (DNS time: … TCP/SSL handshake time: … HTTP Request/Response time: …)'. Meanwhile cron.job_run_details for jobid 2 over 24h returns exactly one status group: succeeded = 288, return_message '1 row' — because net.http_post only ENQUEUES the request, so pg_cron records the enqueue's success and can never observe the HTTP outcome. I pulled the full cron command: it pins `timeout_milliseconds := 20000`, against app/api/cron/route.ts:38 `maxDuration = 60` and processor.ts:72 TIME_BUDGET_MS = 50_000. The function is demonstrably NOT killed by the client disconnect — clean ticks log activity for a mean of 39.2s and up to 46.3s, well past the 20s pg_net gives up at.
verified.impact: Confirmed on both halves. The pg_net response-cleanup churn is fed by a 100% failure rate: the two `WITH rows AS (SELECT ctid FROM net._http_response WHERE created < now…)` cleanup statements account for 6,111,387 + 3,304,226 = 9,415,613 ms (~2.6 hours) of execution, matching the finder's banked figure. Operationally worse is the blindness: cron.job_run_details is the first thing an operator checks, and it is structurally incapable of ever showing a problem — it reported 288/288 succeeded across the same 24h in which 221 ticks were killed mid-round.
verified.recommendation: Raise the cron's timeout_milliseconds to 65000 (above maxDuration 60) so a real status_code is recorded, then alert on net._http_response rows where status_code <> 200 OR error_msg IS NOT NULL. The alternative the finder offers — return 202 immediately and process the batch in a self-invoked call — also removes the response-cleanup cost, but it is a larger change and should not be bundled with the urgent email fixes.
verified.note: Reproduced exactly, including the single-row result shape on both queries and the 20000ms cron parameter.

verified.title: Re-design: the fixes compound — pending 19,733 → ~11, ~270,000 ms/day of DB time recovered, job latency 12+ days → under 5 minutes
verified.evidence: The structural argument holds and the ordering is sound, but two headline numbers do not survive re-measurement. (1) '~610,000 ms/day of DB time removed' is built from 246,528 ms/day for getDistinctPendingTypes plus 363,168 for getQueueDepth. The first is refuted above (real recent cost 15.1 ms/call ≈ 4.3 s/day, not 246,528) and the second is 268,000, not 363,168. Real recoverable DB time is ~270,000 ms/day (4.5 min), not ~610,000. (2) 'Vercel cron function-seconds fall from ~288 × 22s = 6,336 s/day' understates current spend, because a poisoned tick stops logging at 10.5s but keeps running to the 60s maxDuration: true current spend is ≈ 221×60 + 67×40 ≈ 15,900 s/day. The saving from fixing the poison is therefore LARGER than claimed, not smaller. What does reproduce: 288 ticks/day; 1,342 completions/24h (finder said 1,248); 221/288 ticks killed; clean ticks exit on the 40s budget exactly as designed (mean logged span 39.2s); non-email handlers complete in 387-1,006 ms (finder said 384-1,008).
verified.impact: Corrected end state, ordered by leverage per line changed: (1) constant dedup_key on the six types — 6 one-line edits, removes ~19,720 rows and 1,728 junk enqueues/day, and takes every claim scan from up to 10,815 buffers to a handful. (2) SMTP timeouts + deadline check in retryFailedEmails — restores ~221 ticks/day from a truncated round to the full 40s window, worth ~500 job executions/day and roughly 11,000 Vercel function-seconds/day. (3) The email retry-count guard — stops the Resend quota exhaustion, the email_logs growth, and the duplicate emails a real member is receiving. (4) idx_job_queue_claim — makes (1) durable. (5) Merging the two introspection queries — ~268,000 ms/day. (6) Dropping the 'started' log row — halves 451,892 inserts. Pending goes 19,733 → ~11 (-99.94%) and oldest-pending from 16.3 days to under 5 minutes.
verified.recommendation: Ship in this order, each independently deployable: (a) smtp.ts timeouts + tickBudgetExhausted in retryFailedEmails + LIMIT 50→5; (b) the email retry-count guard — do this BEFORE the backlog purge, not after as the finder sequences it, or the 780 currently-eligible failed rows immediately re-amplify; (c) purge the pending email_retry_failed rows; (d) the six constant dedup keys + one-off backlog DELETE; (e) idx_job_queue_claim + split the claim into typed/untyped statements; (f) merge getDistinctPendingTypes and getQueueDepth; (g) 'started'-log removal + job_logs retention; (h) prune index + dedup key; (i) pg_net timeout 20s→65s. Then re-measure completions/tick and per-type oldest_mins. Do NOT add another fairness mechanism — finding 11 establishes the rotation is working.
verified.note: OVERSTATED on the aggregate DB-time saving (~610,000 → ~270,000 ms/day) because it inherits the refuted getDistinctPendingTypes number, and understated on Vercel function-seconds. The prioritisation, the compounding argument and the 'do not touch fairness' conclusion are all sound and I would ship in substantially this order, with the retry-guard moved ahead of the purge.
